title: Comparative Performance Analysis of NIST PQC Standards: From STM32 Software Limitations to FPGA-SoC Acceleration
abstract: The rapid advancement of quantum computing poses a significant threat to classical public-key cryptographic systems, necessitating the transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC). This study investigates the implementation challenges of NISTstandardized signature schemes on resource-constrained embedded hardware. We present a comparative analysis of SPHINCS+ and CRYSTALS-Dilithium on an ARM Cortex-M4 (STM32F407G) microcontroller. Our findings reveal that SPHINCS+ is practically unusable in this software-only environment, with impractical execution times. Furthermore, the reference Dilithium implementation failed to execute entirely on the MCU due to severe RAM and timing constraints. To overcome these hardware limitations, we integrated a hardware-accelerated Dilithium core onto a Xilinx Zynq-7000 ZedBoard SoC. By implementing a specialized Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) accelerator in the FPGA fabric, we achieved successful execution with performance rates for key generation and signature generation at millisecond levels. These results demonstrate that while pure software PQC is non-viable for standard microcontrollers, a hardware-software codesign approach provides the necessary efficiency for quantumresistant embedded systems.
summary: This paper investigates the feasibility of running NIST PQC algorithms like Dilithium and SPHINCS+ on embedded systems. Testing revealed that standard microcontrollers fail due to memory or time constraints. The authors successfully overcame this by integrating an NTT accelerator into an FPGA fabric, proving that hardware-software co-design is essential for practical quantum-resistant embedded security.
main_problem: The study addresses the practical implementation challenges of NIST-standardized Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) signature schemes on resource-constrained embedded hardware.
main_result: Pure software PQC implementations are non-viable for standard microcontrollers due to severe memory and timing limitations; however, a hardware-software co-design approach using FPGA acceleration achieves millisecond performance rates.
method: The authors conducted a comparative performance analysis by implementing SPHINCS+ and CRYSTALS-Dilithium on two platforms: an STM32 microcontroller (software-only) and a Zynq-7000 SoC (hardware/software co-design).
model_or_system: The experimental platforms include the ARM Cortex-M4 based STM32F407G microcontroller and the Xilinx Zynq-7000 ZedBoard SoC, which integrates a processor system with an Artix-7 FPGA fabric for acceleration.
key_observables: Execution times for key generation and signature generation (measured in minutes vs. milliseconds); feasibility of execution under limited SRAM capacity.
important_parameters: The comparison highlights the limitations imposed by 192 KB SRAM on the MCU versus the capability of offloading computationally heavy primitives like NTT to the FPGA fabric.
main_assumptions: The necessity of hardware acceleration is established because general-purpose MCUs lack the necessary resources for high-degree polynomial multiplications required by modern PQC schemes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup of both the STM32F407G and Zynq-7000 boards, alongside schematic representations of the signing procedures for Dilithium and SPHINCS+.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure moving from identifying the quantum threat to testing baseline software performance on an MCU (showing failure), and finally proposing and demonstrating a hardware-software co-design solution using FPGA acceleration to achieve practical performance metrics.
why_interesting: While not directly related to fundamental AMO physics, the rigorous engineering challenge of implementing complex mathematical structures (like polynomial arithmetic in PQC) onto constrained digital hardware shares conceptual parallels with simulating quantum dynamics on limited computational resources.
